title: The House of Wisdom
hookLine: a Baghdad center where scholars translated and studied Greek, Persian and Indian works

cards: A caliph dreams that a man is sitting on his bed: fair-skinned and broad-browed. The caliph asks who he is. Aristotle, the man says.
The caliph asks him, what is good? The dream-Aristotle answers in steps: first, whatever reason finds good; then, whatever the religious law finds good; then, whatever people find good.
The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim tells this story about the caliph al-Ma'mun, Harun's son, as one reason Greek books were sought out and brought to Baghdad.
Whether or not the dream happened, the books really came, and something in Baghdad took them in. It had a name: Bayt al-Hikmah. Today: the House of Wisdom.

teach.b: Bayt al-Hikmah means the House of Wisdom. Start with a caution: historians argue about what it actually was. A palace library?
A translation office? A meeting place for scholars? The sources are thin, and it may have been smaller than its fame.
What isn't in doubt is the work done in Baghdad in those generations.

Books in Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit were turned into Arabic: Euclid's geometry, Ptolemy's astronomy, the medicine of Galen, the philosophy of Aristotle, Persian wisdom literature, Indian astronomy and numbers.
The people doing the work were not all Muslims. One well-known translator, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, was a Christian physician.
In a letter about his work, he describes hunting for several copies of a book by Galen and comparing them before he translated, because copies differ and mistakes creep in.
A later writer, al-Safadi, describes his way as carrying over the meaning of a whole sentence, not swapping word for word.
Muslim scholars took up these books, argued with them, corrected them and built on them, in mathematics, medicine and philosophy. Why would a Muslim court spend so much on foreign books?

teach.h: WISDOM IS A GIFT TO SEEK.
teach.b: Some readers point to the Qur'an, which says God gives wisdom to whom He wills, and that whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. Wisdom, on that view, isn't owned by one people. It's a gift you go looking for.

how: Muslim scholars point to the House of Wisdom and the translation movement when they talk about learning from other peoples, and historians study the surviving Arabic translations and Hunayn's own letter about his work.

games.q: you're Hunayn. you have one copy of a book by Galen, and you're asked to translate it. what do you do?
o: translate your one copy, word for word.
find several copies, compare them, and carry over the meaning.
games.why: in his own letter, Hunayn describes hunting for several copies to compare before translating; a later writer, al-Safadi, says he carried over the meaning, not word for word.

practice: Bring to mind one book, poem or text you've read that was first written in another language, a novel, a scripture, a set of instructions, and the translator who carried those words across, whose name you may not know.
Give them a moment of thanks. If you pray, ask in your own words to recognize wisdom wherever it turns up.

wordCard.voice: Bayt al-Hikmah. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad, linked with the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the House of Wisdom; hikmah, wisdom, is also a word of the Qur'an.

carryVoice: Your line: wisdom from everywhere. Hunayn compared the copies before he trusted one. See you tomorrow.
